question: ¿Qué necesita un agente de código LLM (Claude Code) para ser máximamente efectivo en ingeniería de software real? Investigación para las especificaciones v0.1 de "galaxy-brain", un plugin OSS de Claude Code centrado en un loop de revisión autónomo con evaluador adversarial (generador ≠ evaluador, test-first, gates de suite completa, nunca auto-merge), cubriendo context engineering, memoria persistente, verificación/feedback loops, herramientas deterministas (LSP/AST/análisis estático), spec-driven development, orquestación multi-agente, hooks/routing, evidencia empírica de benchmarks y el ecosistema OSS existente.

angles.label: primaria/autorizada — ingeniería de Anthropic sobre context engineering y memoria de agentes
angles.query: Anthropic engineering blog context engineering Claude Code agents compaction subagents context isolation memory tool best practices
angles.rationale: El blog de ingeniería de Anthropic es la fuente más autorizada sobre cómo el propio harness de Claude Code gestiona compaction, sub-agentes como firewall de contexto y memoria persistente; cubre las palancas (1) y (2) directamente desde quien construye el agente.

angles.label: empírica/benchmarks — qué cambios de scaffold mejoran resultados medibles
angles.query: SWE-bench Verified Terminal-Bench agent scaffold ablation study what actually improves LLM coding agent performance 2025
angles.rationale: Separa evidencia de folklore (palanca 8): ablations y leaderboards reproducibles muestran qué componentes del harness (tests, retrieval, planning, multi-agente) mueven la aguja y cuáles no, base para priorizar por impacto esperado.

angles.label: académica/verificación — evaluador adversarial y sesgos de LLM-as-judge
angles.query: LLM-as-judge self-preference bias generator evaluator model diversity adversarial code review verification paper arXiv
angles.rationale: El núcleo de galaxy-brain es generador ≠ evaluador; los papers sobre sesgos de auto-preferencia, posición y verbosidad en jueces LLM y sobre diversidad de modelos definen cómo diseñar el evaluador para que no valide su propio trabajo (palanca 3).

angles.label: tooling determinista — LSP, AST y análisis estático como gates de agentes
angles.query: tree-sitter LSP static analysis type checker linter integration LLM coding agent deterministic feedback tool effectiveness
angles.rationale: Cubre la palanca 4: qué gana un agente al usar herramientas ejecutables y deterministas (diagnósticos LSP, AST, type-checkers como gates duros) frente a solo leer texto, con estudios y experiencias de implementación.

angles.label: practicante/ecosistema — plugins y harnesses OSS existentes y spec-driven development
angles.query: Claude Code plugins hooks PreToolUse subagents open source autonomous review loop GitHub Spec Kit spec-driven development
angles.rationale: Mapea lo que ya existe en el ecosistema OSS de Claude Code (palancas 5, 6, 7 y 9): hooks/routing, orquestación multi-agente, Spec Kit y harnesses de revisión, imprescindible para diferenciarse y no reinventar en la v0.1.

summary_from_scope: Divido la pregunta en cinco frentes complementarios: la fuente primaria autorizada (ingeniería de Anthropic sobre context engineering y memoria de agentes), la evidencia empírica de benchmarks que separa mejoras reales de folklore, la literatura académica sobre evaluadores adversariales y sesgos de LLM-as-judge, la integración de herramientas deterministas como gates de verificación, y el panorama práctico del ecosistema OSS (plugins, hooks, spec-driven) para diferenciación. Cada query apunta a un tipo de fuente distinto (blog de ingeniería, papers/leaderboards, arXiv, estudios de tooling, repos con tracción) para minimizar solapamiento.

claims.claim: GPT-4, when used as an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, exhibits a significant degree of self-preference bias, measured via a novel quantitative metric the authors introduce.
claims.quote: In this paper, we introduce a novel quantitative metric to measure the self-preference bias. Our experimental results demonstrate that GPT-4 exhibits a significant degree of self-preference bias.

claims.claim: LLM evaluators assign significantly higher evaluations than human evaluators to outputs with lower perplexity, and this effect holds regardless of whether the outputs were generated by the evaluator model itself.
claims.quote: Our findings reveal that LLMs assign significantly higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity than human evaluators, regardless of whether the outputs were self-generated.

claims.claim: The root cause of self-preference bias is familiarity as measured by perplexity — LLMs prefer texts more familiar to them — rather than mere authorship recognition, which implies that simply using a different model as evaluator does not fully eliminate the bias if outputs remain low-perplexity for the judge.
claims.quote: This suggests that the essence of the bias lies in perplexity and that the self-preference bias exists because LLMs prefer texts more familiar to them.

claims.claim: Prior to this work there was no established quantitative method for measuring self-preference bias in LLM judges, and its underlying causes were poorly understood.
claims.quote: Despite the importance of this issue, there is a lack of established methods to measure the self-preference bias quantitatively, and its underlying causes are poorly understood.

claims.claim: The paper was peer-reviewed and accepted at the NeurIPS 2024 Safe Generative AI Workshop, lending it more credibility than an unreviewed preprint.
claims.quote: Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2024 Safe Generative AI Workshop

claims.claim: En una evaluación interna de búsqueda agéntica de Anthropic, combinar el memory tool con context editing mejoró el rendimiento del agente un 39% sobre baseline, y context editing por sí solo aportó un 29% de mejora — evidencia empírica directa (aunque interna, no reproducible públicamente) de que la gestión de contexto es una palanca de alto impacto para agentes.
claims.quote: On an internal evaluation set for agentic search, we tested how context management improves agent performance on complex, multi-step tasks. The results demonstrate significant gains: combining the memory tool with context editing improved performance by 39% over baseline. Context editing alone delivered a 29% improvement.

claims.claim: En una evaluación de búsqueda web de 100 turnos, context editing permitió completar workflows que de otro modo fallarían por agotamiento de contexto, reduciendo el consumo de tokens en un 84% — cuantifica el beneficio de limpiar tool calls/results obsoletos en tareas de larga duración.
claims.quote: In a 100-turn web search evaluation, context editing enabled agents to complete workflows that would otherwise fail due to context exhaustion—while reducing token consumption by 84%.

claims.claim: La arquitectura de memoria persistente que Anthropic eligió para producción es file-based y client-side (no vectorial): Claude crea/lee/actualiza/borra archivos en un directorio de memoria gestionado por el desarrollador, que persiste entre conversaciones — respaldo directo a la decisión de diseño 'memoria basada en archivos' frente a stores vectoriales.
claims.quote: The memory tool enables Claude to store and consult information outside the context window through a file-based system. Claude can create, read, update, and delete files in a dedicated memory directory stored in your infrastructure that persists across conversations. [...] The memory tool operates entirely client-side through tool calls. Developers manage the storage backend, giving them complete control over where the data is stored and how it's persisted.

claims.claim: Context editing funciona eliminando automáticamente tool calls y resultados obsoletos al acercarse a los límites de tokens, y Anthropic afirma que esto no solo extiende la duración del agente sino que aumenta el rendimiento efectivo del modelo al enfocarse solo en contexto relevante (consistente con el fenómeno de 'context rot').
claims.quote: Context editing automatically clears stale tool calls and results from within the context window when approaching token limits. [...] This also increases the effective model performance as Claude focuses only on relevant context.

claims.claim: Para el caso de uso de coding, Anthropic prescribe el patrón: context editing limpia lecturas de archivos y resultados de tests antiguos mientras la memoria persiste insights de debugging y decisiones arquitectónicas — un patrón directamente trasladable al diseño del loop de revisión de galaxy-brain (qué descartar vs qué persistir entre iteraciones).
claims.quote: Coding: Context editing clears old file reads and test results while memory preserves debugging insights and architectural decisions, enabling agents to work on large codebases without losing progress.

claims.claim: Anthropic afirma que Claude Code opera con un loop de feedback específico de tres fases — recopilar contexto, actuar, verificar el trabajo, repetir — y que este loop es el marco recomendado para diseñar las capacidades de cualquier agente construido sobre el Claude Agent SDK.
claims.quote: In Claude Code, Claude often operates in a specific feedback loop: gather context -> take action -> verify work -> repeat.

claims.claim: El Claude Agent SDK incluye una función de compaction que resume automáticamente los mensajes previos cuando se acerca el límite de contexto, construida sobre el comando /compact de Claude Code, como mecanismo para que agentes de larga duración no agoten el contexto.
claims.quote: The Claude Agent SDK's compact feature automatically summarizes previous messages when the context limit approaches, so your agent won't run out of context.

claims.claim: Anthropic afirma que los subagentes sirven como aislamiento de contexto (context firewall): usan ventanas de contexto propias y aisladas y solo devuelven al orquestador la información relevante en lugar de su contexto completo, lo que los hace ideales para tareas que requieren filtrar grandes volúmenes de información; además habilitan paralelización.
claims.quote: Second, they help manage context: subagents use their own isolated context windows, and only send relevant information back to the orchestrator, rather than their full context. This makes them ideal for tasks that require sifting through large amounts of information where most of it won't be useful.

claims.claim: Anthropic sostiene que la mejor forma de verificación es el feedback determinista basado en reglas (como linting), y afirma concretamente que suele ser mejor generar TypeScript y lintearlo que generar JavaScript puro porque aporta capas adicionales de feedback — evidencia a favor de gates deterministas (linters, type-checkers) sobre verificación puramente basada en LLM.
claims.quote: The best form of feedback is providing clearly defined rules for an output, then explaining which rules failed and why. [...] it is usually better to generate TypeScript and lint it than it is to generate pure JavaScript because it provides you with multiple additional layers of feedback.

claims.claim: Anthropic advierte explícitamente que LLM-as-judge (usar otro modelo para juzgar la salida del agente con reglas difusas) generalmente NO es un método muy robusto y tiene costes fuertes de latencia, aunque puede aportar mejoras cuando cualquier ganancia de rendimiento justifica el coste — relevante para calibrar el diseño del evaluador adversarial de galaxy-brain y no depender solo del juez LLM.
claims.quote: You can also have another language model "judge" the output of your agent based on fuzzy rules. This is generally not a very robust method, and can have heavy latency tradeoffs, but for applications where any boost in performance is worth the cost, it can be helpful.

claims.claim: LLM-as-judge pairwise rankings can be flipped simply by swapping the order in which candidate responses appear in the prompt: with ChatGPT as evaluator, order manipulation made Vicuna-13B appear to beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 Vicuna Benchmark queries. This means any galaxy-brain evaluator loop that compares two candidates in one prompt must control for positional bias.
claims.quote: We find that the quality ranking of candidate responses can be easily hacked by simply altering their order of appearance in the context. This manipulation allows us to skew the evaluation result, making one model appear considerably superior to the other, e.g., Vicuna-13B could beat ChatGPT on 66 over 80 tested queries with ChatGPT as an evaluator.

claims.claim: Positional bias is systematic and measurable, and weaker evaluator models are more affected: when response order was swapped, GPT-4 contradicted its own verdict at conflict rates of 46.3% and 5.0% (two template settings), while ChatGPT's conflict rates were 82.5% and 52.5% — evidence that evaluator model strength matters when choosing the judge in a generator≠evaluator setup.
claims.quote: We found that GPT-4 exhibited conflict rates of 46.3% and 5.0%, respectively. In contrast, ChatGPT displayed considerably higher conflict rates, with figures of 82.5% and 52.5%, respectively. These findings indicate that LLMs can be self-conflicting due to the sensitivity of the response order in the template, with stronger models being less influenced by the placement of responses.

claims.claim: Two cheap prompt-level calibrations — Multiple Evidence Calibration (generate multiple evaluation rationales before scoring) and Balanced Position Calibration (aggregate scores across both response orders) — measurably improve judge-human agreement: ChatGPT's accuracy against human labels improved by 14.3% and its kappa rose from 0.06 to 0.31. These are directly implementable techniques for a plugin's adversarial evaluator.
claims.quote: by employing the MEC and BPC calibration strategies, ChatGPT demonstrates a notable improvement in both accuracy and the kappa correlation coefficient. Specifically, the accuracy is improved by 14.3%, and the kappa correlation coefficient is increased from 0.06 to 0.31

claims.claim: Running the judgment in both positions and aggregating (BPC) beats simply sampling more judgments in a fixed order: MEC(k=3)+BPC(k=3) outperformed MEC(k=6), confirming positional bias is a distinct error source that swapping-and-aggregating specifically corrects — a concrete design rule for an evaluation gate (swap candidate order, not just re-sample).
claims.quote: “MEC (k=3) + BPC (k=3)” outperforms “MEC (k=6)”, demonstrating that LLMs are affected by positional bias, and BPC effectively ensures that LLMs serve as fair evaluators

claims.claim: Even human annotators agree only moderately with each other (average accuracy 71.7%, kappa 0.54 versus the majority vote), and GPT-4 aligns with human judgments better than ChatGPT — bounding the realistic ceiling for any automatic evaluator and supporting the choice of the strongest available model as the judge.
claims.quote: the average accuracy and the kappa correlation coefficient of human annotations are 71.7% and 0.54, respectively; 2) Overall, GPT-4 achieves higher alignment with human judgments compared with ChatGPT, showing its powerful alignment ability with humans

claims.claim: Anthropic's API offers first-party, server-side implementations of all three core context-management primitives — compaction (identifier compact_20260112, beta header compact-2026-01-12, default trigger 150K tokens), tool-result clearing (clear_tool_uses_20250919, beta header context-management-2025-06-27, default trigger 100K tokens, keeps last 3 tool uses by default), and a memory tool (memory_20250818, no beta header) — so agent builders can adopt them without custom orchestration infrastructure. A plugin like galaxy-brain could delegate these to the API rather than reimplementing them.
claims.quote: They also all have first-party API support, so you can adopt them without building orchestration infrastructure. ... Compaction | compact_20260112 | compact-2026-01-12 | Token threshold (server-side, min 50K) | trigger (default 150K), instructions, pause_after_compaction ... Tool clearing | clear_tool_uses_20250919 | context-management-2025-06-27 | Token threshold (server-side) | trigger (default 100K), keep (default 3 tool uses), clear_at_least, exclude_tools, clear_tool_inputs | Memory tool | memory_20250818 | none (standalone) | The model (it's a tool call) | Client implements
claims._publishDate: Not explicitly stated on page; references the compact-2026-01-12 API beta and Sonnet/Opus 4.6, implying publication in or after January 2026

claims.claim: Context degradation ('context rot') begins before the hard token limit: as tokens in the context window increase, the model's recall accuracy over that context decreases, which motivates proactive context pruning in long-horizon agents rather than only reacting at the limit.
claims.quote: Studies on needle-in-a-haystack style benchmarking have uncovered the concept of context rot: as the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model's ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases. So, even before the hard context limit is reached, the agent may be getting less out of each token.
claims._publishDate: Not explicitly stated on page; references the compact-2026-01-12 API beta and Sonnet/Opus 4.6, implying publication in or after January 2026

claims.claim: The three primitives trade fidelity differently and compose rather than compete: tool-result clearing is lossless only when the tool is re-callable, compaction is controlled-lossy (the summarizer prompt determines what survives), and memory is lossless on saved content but bounded by the agent's judgment about what to save — clearing/compaction manage the in-window budget while memory provides cross-session persistence.
claims.quote: Clearing is lossless as long as the tool is re-callable. Compaction is lossy in a controlled way: the summarizer prompt (default or custom) determines what survives. Memory is lossless on what gets saved but is only as good as the agent's judgment about what to save. Each primitive trades fidelity differently.
claims._publishDate: Not explicitly stated on page; references the compact-2026-01-12 API beta and Sonnet/Opus 4.6, implying publication in or after January 2026

claims.claim: Claude Code in production uses compaction plus two complementary file-based memory systems: developer-authored CLAUDE.md files checked into source control (coding standards, architecture, workflows) and 'auto memory' that Claude writes itself (build commands, debugging insights, preferences learned from corrections) — evidence that file-based memory architectures are what ships in production, relevant to galaxy-brain's persistent-memory design choice.
claims.quote: Claude Code is a real-world example that employs compaction alongside two complementary memory systems: CLAUDE.md files hold user-defined instructions and rules (coding standards, project architecture, workflows) that the developer writes and checks into source control; auto memory holds learnings and patterns Claude writes itself (build commands, debugging insights, preferences discovered from corrections).
claims._publishDate: Not explicitly stated on page; references the compact-2026-01-12 API beta and Sonnet/Opus 4.6, implying publication in or after January 2026

claims.claim: Beyond the three primitives, Anthropic identifies subagents (isolating work in separate context windows) and programmatic tool calling (keeping large results out of the window entirely) as additional context-engineering levers; in the cookbook's controlled two-session experiment, the memory tool let session 2 skip 4 file reads by pulling session 1's findings from /memories, but the benefit collapses if the prior session saved sparse or poorly organized notes.
claims.quote: There are several levers for this: subagents that isolate work in their own context, programmatic tool calling that keeps large results out of the window entirely, and others. ... Memory saved 4 file read(s): the agent pulled Session 1's findings from /memories instead of re-reading the source documents. ... If Session 1 had saved sparse or poorly organized notes, Session 2 would fall back to re-reading source documents. Memory's value depends on the agent's judgment about what to write.
claims._publishDate: Not explicitly stated on page; references the compact-2026-01-12 API beta and Sonnet/Opus 4.6, implying publication in or after January 2026

claims.claim: El contexto es un recurso finito con rendimientos marginales decrecientes: existe 'context rot' — a medida que crece el número de tokens en la ventana de contexto, la capacidad del modelo para recuperar información con precisión decrece, y esto ocurre en todos los modelos (no es específico de uno). Implicación para galaxy-brain: minimizar tokens en contexto es una palanca de rendimiento medible, no una preferencia estética.
claims.quote: Studies on needle-in-a-haystack style benchmarking have uncovered the concept of context rot: as the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model's ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases. While some models exhibit more gentle degradation than others, this characteristic emerges across all models. Context, therefore, must be treated as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns.

claims.claim: Los sub-agentes funcionan como 'firewall de contexto': cada sub-agente puede explorar usando decenas de miles de tokens pero devuelve al agente principal solo un resumen destilado de ~1.000-2.000 tokens, y Anthropic reporta que este patrón mostró una mejora sustancial sobre sistemas de agente único en tareas complejas de investigación (referenciando su sistema multi-agente de research).
claims.quote: Each subagent might explore extensively, using tens of thousands of tokens or more, but returns only a condensed, distilled summary of its work (often 1,000-2,000 tokens). This approach achieves a clear separation of concerns—the detailed search context remains isolated within sub-agents, while the lead agent focuses on synthesizing and analyzing the results. This pattern, discussed in How we built our multi-agent research system, showed a substantial improvement over single-agent systems on complex research tasks.

claims.claim: La compaction de Claude Code está implementada de forma concreta y replicable: se pasa el historial de mensajes al modelo para resumirlo preservando decisiones arquitectónicas, bugs no resueltos y detalles de implementación, descartando outputs de herramientas redundantes, y el agente continúa con ese resumen más los 5 archivos accedidos más recientemente; además, el 'tool result clearing' es la forma más segura y ligera de compaction. Receta de tuning: primero maximizar recall en trazas complejas, luego iterar precisión.
claims.quote: In Claude Code, for example, we implement this by passing the message history to the model to summarize and compress the most critical details. The model preserves architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, and implementation details while discarding redundant tool outputs or messages. The agent can then continue with this compressed context plus the five most recently accessed files.

claims.claim: La memoria persistente que Anthropic respalda para agentes es file-based (no vectorial): el memory tool lanzado con Sonnet 4.5 almacena y consulta información fuera de la ventana de contexto mediante un sistema de archivos, y el note-taking estructurado (p.ej. un NOTES.md o to-do list) permite mantener estado entre resets de contexto y sesiones — demostrado empíricamente en Claude plays Pokémon manteniendo coherencia a través de miles de pasos sin prompting sobre estructura de memoria.
claims.quote: we released a memory tool in public beta on the Claude Developer Platform that makes it easier to store and consult information outside the context window through a file-based system. This allows agents to build up knowledge bases over time, maintain project state across sessions, and reference previous work without keeping everything in context.

claims.claim: La estrategia de recuperación 'just-in-time' con identificadores ligeros (rutas de archivo, queries guardadas, enlaces) que cargan datos dinámicamente en runtime es la que usa Claude Code, en lugar de pre-cargar todo el contexto vía embeddings; los metadatos (jerarquías de carpetas, convenciones de nombres, timestamps) actúan como señales de relevancia, con el trade-off explícito de que la exploración en runtime es más lenta que la recuperación pre-computada.
claims.quote: Rather than pre-processing all relevant data up front, agents built with the "just in time" approach maintain lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, web links, etc.) and use these references to dynamically load data into context at runtime using tools. Anthropic's agentic coding solution Claude Code uses this approach to perform complex data analysis over large databases.

claims.claim: En benchmarks verificables (razonamiento matemático, conocimiento factual, generación de código), el sesgo de auto-preferencia dañino persiste específicamente cuando el modelo evaluador se equivoca como generador, y los modelos más fuertes muestran un sesgo dañino MÁS pronunciado cuando fallan — es decir, un modelo es sistemáticamente malo detectando sus propios errores, lo que justifica empíricamente separar generador y evaluador (generador ≠ evaluador) en un loop de revisión.
claims.quote: Harmful self-preference persists when evaluator models err as generators, and stronger models display more pronounced harmful self-preference bias when they do err. This suggests stronger models struggle more to recognize when they are wrong.

claims.claim: La auto-preferencia de los modelos fuertes es en su mayoría legítima (favorecen sus salidas porque son objetivamente mejores), no puramente sesgo: usar el mismo modelo como juez no es uniformemente dañino, solo lo es en el subconjunto de casos donde el generador se equivocó — matiz importante para no sobredimensionar la diversidad de modelos como palanca.
claims.quote: While stronger models exhibit greater self-preference, much of this preference aligns with objectively superior performance, indicating stronger models prefer themselves mostly legitimately.

claims.claim: El escalado en tiempo de inferencia del evaluador — en concreto, generar una cadena de razonamiento (Chain-of-Thought) larga antes de emitir el veredicto — reduce de forma efectiva la auto-preferencia dañina; para galaxy-brain esto implica que el evaluador adversarial debe razonar extensamente antes de aprobar/rechazar, no dar un veredicto directo.
claims.quote: Inference-time scaling strategies, such as generating a long Chain-of-Thought before evaluation, effectively reduce the harmful self-preference.

claims.claim: Recomendación práctica del paper: antes de desplegar un LLM como evaluador en un dominio, hay que medir su rendimiento GENERATIVO en ese dominio, porque la capacidad generativa predice la fiabilidad del juicio; en sistemas grandes conviene enrutar cada evaluación al modelo con mayor capacidad generativa en el dominio específico.
claims.quote: before deploying an LLM as an evaluator for a specific task or domain, its generative performance on the target domain should be rigorously assessed. This pre-assessment helps select models that are more likely to provide accurate judgments and exhibit more legitimate (rather than harmful) preference.

claims.claim: La metodología distingue auto-preferencia dañina de legítima usando benchmarks con ground truth objetivo (incluida generación de código) en experimentos a gran escala sobre 7 familias de modelos (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, GPT, DeepSeek), y la revisión v3 extiende los hallazgos a dominios subjetivos reales vía LMArena — lo que da a estas conclusiones más solidez que estudios previos basados solo en tareas subjetivas.
claims.quote: we investigate self-preference using verifiable benchmarks (mathematical reasoning, factual knowledge, code generation) that allow objective ground-truth assessment. This enables us to distinguish harmful (favoring objectively worse responses) from legitimate (favoring genuinely superior ones) self-preference. Our large-scale experiments across 7 model families reveal three key findings

claims.claim: A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as orchestrator and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research eval, especially on breadth-first queries with multiple independent directions.
claims.quote: We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval.

claims.claim: In Anthropic's analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance, and together with number of tool calls and model choice explained 95% — implying multi-agent gains come mainly from spending more tokens across parallel context windows.
claims.quote: In our analysis, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation... We found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory factors.

claims.claim: Multi-agent systems consume roughly 15x the tokens of chat interactions, and Anthropic explicitly states most coding tasks are a poor fit for multi-agent architectures today because they are less parallelizable and agents coordinate poorly in real time — directly relevant to when galaxy-brain should NOT fan out agents.
claims.quote: agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. ... most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time.

claims.claim: For long-horizon agent sessions, Anthropic's production pattern is: summarize completed work phases into external memory, spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts when the context limit approaches, and have subagents write outputs directly to a filesystem and pass lightweight references to avoid lossy relay through the coordinator ('game of telephone').
claims.quote: We implemented patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs.

claims.claim: For LLM-as-judge evaluation, a single LLM call with one rubric prompt (factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency) outputting a 0.0-1.0 score plus pass-fail was more consistent and better aligned with human judgment than using multiple specialized judges; for state-mutating agents, end-state evaluation with checkpoint state changes beat turn-by-turn process validation.
claims.quote: We experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component, but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.

claims.claim: Context compaction alone is insufficient for long-running agent work: even Opus 4.5 running on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows fails to build a production-quality web app from only a high-level prompt, exhibiting two failure modes (attempting to one-shot the app and running out of context mid-feature, or prematurely declaring the project done).
claims.quote: However, compaction isn't sufficient. Out of the box, even a frontier coding model like Opus 4.5 running on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows will fall short of building a production-quality web app if it's only given a high-level prompt, such as "build a clone of claude.ai."

claims.claim: A two-part harness architecture — an initializer agent that sets up file-based memory artifacts (an init.sh script, a claude-progress.txt log, an initial git commit) plus a coding agent prompted to make incremental progress and leave structured updates — enables agents to bridge sessions; state recovery is achieved via plain files and git history, not vector stores.
claims.quote: Initializer agent: The very first agent session uses a specialized prompt that asks the model to set up the initial environment: an `init.sh` script, a claude-progress.txt file that keeps a log of what agents have done, and an initial git commit that shows what files were added. ... The key insight here was finding a way for agents to quickly understand the state of work when starting with a fresh context window, which is accomplished with the claude-progress.txt file alongside the git history.

claims.claim: A structured JSON feature list (200+ end-to-end feature descriptions, all initialized as failing, editable only via a 'passes' field with strongly-worded no-edit instructions) prevents premature completion claims; Anthropic found empirically that models are less likely to inappropriately modify JSON files than Markdown files.
claims.quote: We prompt coding agents to edit this file only by changing the status of a passes field, and we use strongly-worded instructions like "It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests because this could lead to missing or buggy functionality." After some experimentation, we landed on using JSON for this, as the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files compared to Markdown files.

claims.claim: Without explicit prompting, Claude marks features complete after only unit tests or curl checks that miss end-to-end failures; giving it browser-automation testing tools (Puppeteer MCP) and requiring testing 'as a human user would' dramatically improved performance, though tool blind spots (e.g., browser-native alert modals invisible to Puppeteer MCP) correlate with buggier features.
claims.quote: Providing Claude with these kinds of testing tools dramatically improved performance, as the agent was able to identify and fix bugs that weren't obvious from the code alone. ... Claude can't see browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP, and features relying on these modals tended to be buggier as a result.

claims.claim: Working on exactly one feature per session, committing to git with descriptive messages, and writing progress summaries was critical to fixing the do-too-much failure mode and enabled reverting bad changes; meanwhile Anthropic explicitly states it remains an open question whether a multi-agent architecture (testing agent, QA agent, cleanup agent) outperforms a single general-purpose coding agent.
claims.quote: This incremental approach turned out to be critical to addressing the agent's tendency to do too much at once. ... it's still unclear whether a single, general-purpose coding agent performs best across contexts, or if better performance can be achieved through a multi-agent architecture.

claims.claim: When the LLM judge is related to the model that generated the training/synthetic data (same model, inheritance, or same family), the judge shows a systematic, quantified bias toward its related 'student' model: e.g., average preference-leakage scores of 23.6% (Mistral-7B students) and 27.9% (Qwen-2.5-14B students) for the GPT-4o vs Gemini-1.5 generator/judge pair on Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval 2.0 — directly supporting the design rule that the adversarial evaluator must be a different model from the generator.
claims.quote: in most model pairs (except Mistral-GPT-4o vs Mistral-LLaMA-3.3 and Qwen-GPT-4o vs Qwen-LLaMA-3.3), the judge LLMs exhibit a strong preference toward their related student models, leading to large positive values in the preference leakage scores. This finding suggests that preference leakage, along with the resulting bias, is widespread in SFT when the data generator and evaluator are the same.

claims.claim: The bias scales with the degree of relatedness between generator and judge: same model yields ~23.6% average preference-leakage score, an inheritance relationship yields 19.3–22.3%, and same-family models yield ~8.9% — implying that for generator≠evaluator setups, maximum independence (different model family/vendor) reduces but does not fully eliminate judge bias.
claims.quote: Same Model | 28.7% | 18.4% | 23.6% ... Inheritance - w/ same ins. | 17.8% | 20.7% | 19.3% ... Inheritance - w/ different ins. | 18.3% | 26.3% | 22.3% ... Same Family - w/ same series | 10.1% | 7.6% | 8.9%

claims.claim: Preference leakage is harder to detect than previously known judge biases (e.g., egocentric bias): judge LLMs recognize their related student models' outputs at roughly random-guess accuracy (29.8%–53.2%), even though a fine-tuned BERT classifier can identify which generator produced a response with 82.4% accuracy — meaning stylistic fingerprints exist but the judge itself cannot see them, so the bias cannot be prompted away by asking the judge to self-monitor.
claims.quote: the recognition performance of each judge LLM in the content of related students is poor, with accuracy around the performance of random guesses. This suggests that preference leakage is subtler and harder-to-detect for judge LLMs, in contrast to the more obvious egocentric bias.

claims.claim: Judge bias from preference leakage is smallest on objective questions with definitive answers (e.g., mathematical) and largest on subjective questions and judgment dimensions — with programming explicitly classified among the more-leakage-prone subjective categories — which supports anchoring a code-review loop in deterministic verification gates (tests, type-checkers, full-suite runs) rather than unconstrained LLM judgment.
claims.quote: objective questions with a definitive answer, like mathematical ones, demonstrate the least preference leakage. By contrast, subjective questions that have more than one standard answer, such as programming and writing, usually lead to a more obvious preference leakage.

claims.claim: Simple prompt-level mitigations do not fix judge bias — explicitly instructing the judge to be impartial slightly worsened their Error Bias metric (17.8 → 18.3) and paraphrasing also failed (18.7), while chain-of-thought helped modestly (15.6) and contextual calibration with a held-out set was the only strongly effective mitigation (17.8 → 7.3).
claims.quote: Base | 17.8 | + Prompting | 18.3 | + Chain-of-Thought | 15.6 | + Paraphrase | 18.7 | + Auto Calibration | 20.7 | + Contextual Calibration | 7.3 ... contextual calibration with an additional held‑out set for bias adjustment is the most effective, reducing Error Bias from 17.8 to 7.3.

claims.claim: Across several open-source and industrial LLMs, models are NOT reliably better at discriminating (judging) among their own previously-generated responses than at generating initial responses, which undermines the premise that an LLM can improve its output purely via its own judgment (i.e., pure self-review loops where generator = evaluator).
claims.quote: In our resulting experimental analysis of several open-source and industrial LLMs, we observe that models are not reliably better at discriminating among previously-generated alternatives than generating initial responses. This finding challenges the notion that LLMs may be able to enhance their performance only through their own judgment.
claims._publishDate: 2024-04 (arXiv:2404.04298 submitted April 2024; content retrieved from v3 revision)

claims.claim: In 54 out of 56 experiments (covering Phi-3, LLaMA series, Mixtral series, and GPT series on math, world knowledge, truthful QA, and instruction following), the statistical test failed to reject the hypothesis that discrimination is no better than generation; the discrimination-generation difference (DG-Diff) was generally small or negative.
claims.quote: Based on the results in Table 2, in 54 out of 56 experiments, the p-value exceeded the significance level (0.05), leading to the failure to reject the Self-[In]Correct hypothesis. In fact, DG-Diff is generally small or negative across both pre-trained models and aligned models.
claims._publishDate: 2024-04 (arXiv:2404.04298 submitted April 2024; content retrieved from v3 revision)

claims.claim: Prompt-engineering interventions do not fix the self-discrimination deficit: adding more in-context learning examples and chain-of-thought demonstrations leaves the discrimination-generation gap small or negative, so a review loop cannot rely on better judge prompts alone.
claims.quote: Our findings indicate that Self-[In]Correct persists with the inclusion of additional in-context learning examples and chain-of-thought demonstrations.
claims._publishDate: 2024-04 (arXiv:2404.04298 submitted April 2024; content retrieved from v3 revision)

claims.claim: When external ground-truth feedback is available (e.g., tool interactions, test results), LLMs CAN effectively self-improve — the failure is specific to intrinsic self-judgment without external signal, supporting designs that gate on deterministic verification (tests, linters, type-checkers) rather than on the model's own opinion.
claims.quote: The success stories mentioned in previous paragraph show that when external ground-truth feedback is available, LLMs can effectively engage in self-improvement. Gou et al. (2024) shows that LLMs can verify and correct their initial responses through interactions with various external tools.
claims._publishDate: 2024-04 (arXiv:2404.04298 submitted April 2024; content retrieved from v3 revision)

claims.claim: Stronger models tend to have better discrimination ability relative to generation (larger DG-Diff), which supports assigning the evaluator/judge role to the strongest available model and using a different (stronger) model than the generator in adversarial review loops.
claims.quote: Stronger models tend to be better at discrimination (larger DG-Diff).
claims._publishDate: 2024-04 (arXiv:2404.04298 submitted April 2024; content retrieved from v3 revision)

claims.claim: An iterative prompting loop that feeds static analysis findings (from Bandit and Pylint) back to the LLM measurably improves the quality of generated code across security, readability, and reliability dimensions — validating deterministic analyzers as an effective feedback/gate mechanism for code agents.
claims.quote: We introduce an iterative static analysis-driven prompting algorithm that leverages Bandit and Pylint to identify and resolve code quality issues. Our experiments with GPT-4o show substantial improvements

claims.claim: With GPT-4o on the PythonSecurityEval benchmark, the static-analysis feedback loop reduced security issues from over 40% to 13% within ten iterations.
claims.quote: security issues reduced from >40% to 13% ... within ten iterations

claims.claim: The same loop reduced readability violations from over 80% to 11% and reliability warnings from over 50% to 11% within ten iterations, showing the technique generalizes across multiple non-functional quality dimensions, not just security.
claims.quote: readability violations from >80% to 11%, and reliability warnings from >50% to 11% within ten iterations

claims.claim: Standard code-generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP) measure only functional correctness and miss security, reliability, readability, and maintainability — implying an agent harness needs quality gates beyond passing tests.
claims.quote: these benchmarks primarily assess functional correctness and neglect broader dimensions of code quality, including security, reliability, readability, and maintainability

claims.claim: LLMs left unguided produce code where more than 40% of samples contain security issues and more than 80% contain readability violations (baseline before feedback), quantifying why a review loop with deterministic tooling is needed rather than trusting single-shot generation.
claims.quote: security issues reduced from >40% to 13%, readability violations from >80% to 11%, and reliability warnings from >50% to 11%

claims.claim: The adversarial-review skill implements generator≠evaluator with cross-vendor model diversity: Claude Code is the executor/fixer while an external OpenAI Codex model (default gpt-5.5, reasoning effort high) acts as the adversarial reviewer, invoked via Codex CLI (>= 0.132.0) rather than a second Claude instance.
claims.quote: Sends current work for adversarial review through an external AI model (OpenAI Codex by default). Auto-detects what to review: plan or code. Claude fixes issues based on reviewer feedback and resubmits until approved. Maximum 5 rounds.

claims.claim: The review loop is gated by a machine-parseable verdict contract: the reviewer's last line must be exactly 'VERDICT: APPROVED' or 'VERDICT: REVISE', a REVISE verdict must include at least one structured finding tagged [severity: critical|high|medium], and the fix-and-resubmit loop is hard-capped at 5 rounds (not configurable).
claims.quote: Verdict rules: approve if no findings or all low severity; revise if any high/critical. Choose exactly one. The LAST line of your response must be one of: VERDICT: APPROVED / VERDICT: REVISE

claims.claim: The skill supports three auto-detected review modes — plan (review the plan before code exists), code (git diff review), and code-vs-plan (verify implementation matches the plan) — with mode inferred from git state and conversation context, which its author cites as a key differentiator from openai/codex-plugin-cc, whose adversarial prompt structure (XML sections, attack surface checklist, finding bar, calibration rules) it borrowed.
claims.quote: What we did differently: Iterative loop — Claude fixes issues and resubmits (not "stop and ask user"); Plan review — reviews plans before code, not just code; Minimal install — SKILL.md + one references/runner.md, no server, no broker, vs 15+ JS modules; Verbatim output — reviewer findings shown as-is, not rephrased

claims.claim: The skill uses a Sonnet-model runner subagent as a context firewall: the main Claude thread never reads the ~12K-token runner spec or Codex stdout/stderr, receiving only a structured JSON result file path, which the README claims saves ~12K tokens of main-thread context per round across up to 5 rounds.
claims.quote: This keeps runner.md (~12K) out of main's context — both the Read result AND the Agent prompt duplication. Saves ~12K per round × up to 5 rounds per review.

claims.claim: The reviewer is constrained to an auditor role that may execute verification commands (tests, linters, builds) in a bwrap-sandboxed workspace-write mode but must never mutate project files — enforced primarily by a prompt contract plus a git-porcelain mutation snapshot, with an explicitly documented residual gap for already-dirty tracked files; the repo offers no empirical benchmark results for the approach and has modest traction (16 stars, 3 forks, Apache-2.0, created April 2026).
claims.quote: You are an auditor, not a contributor. The lead applies fixes; you find issues.

claims.claim: A mid-tier judge model with the right debiasing strategy can outperform frontier judges at ~15x lower cost: Gemini 2.5 Flash with the 'Combined Budget' strategy achieved the highest human-agreement of all tested configurations (71.0%, kappa=0.549) at ~$0.001/eval, versus Claude Sonnet 4 at 69.5% and ~$0.015/eval — directly relevant to choosing the evaluator model for galaxy-brain's adversarial review loop.
claims.quote: Our headline practical finding is that a mid-tier model with the right debiasing can outperform frontier judges at a fraction of the cost: Gemini 2.5 Flash with the Combined Budget strategy reaches the highest agreement of any configuration we tested (71.0%, kappa=0.549) at ~$0.001 per evaluation, about 15x cheaper than the best frontier setup (Claude Sonnet 4, 69.5%, ~$0.015).

claims.claim: Style bias (judges favoring markdown-formatted answers over plain prose) is the dominant LLM-judge bias, measured at 0.10-0.76 across five models, far exceeding position bias (<=0.04) — implying that an adversarial code evaluator must control for output formatting, not just answer order.
claims.quote: Style bias is the dominant bias (0.10-0.76 across models, favoring markdown over plain prose), far exceeding position bias (<=0.04), yet is rarely studied.

claims.claim: Specific debiasing strategies yield statistically significant agreement gains that survive Holm-Bonferroni correction: Claude with strategy S8 gains +11.5 percentage points, Gemini Flash S8 +7.5pp, Claude S5 (chain-of-thought) +7.3pp, plus Flash S1 (position swap, +4.7pp) and Llama S8 (+4.5pp) — i.e., cheap prompting/aggregation wrappers measurably improve judge reliability.
claims.quote: Debiasing helps multiple models: Claude S8 (+11.5 pp), Flash S8 (+7.5 pp), and Claude S5 (+7.3 pp) survive Holm-Bonferroni correction, with Flash S1 (+4.7 pp) and Llama S8 (+4.5 pp) also significant.

claims.claim: Verbosity bias is heterogeneous by model family when measured length-aware: Gemini Pro/Flash and Llama prefer longer answers (+0.24 to +0.44), Claude prefers concise answers (-0.12), and GPT-4o is neutral (-0.04) — relevant to generator/evaluator model-diversity pairing, since each judge family imports a different length prior.
claims.quote: Verbosity bias is heterogeneous when measured length-aware: Pro, Flash, and Llama prefer longer answers (+0.24 to +0.44), Claude prefers concise (-0.12), and GPT-4o is neutral (-0.04); on truncation controls all models correctly prefer the complete response (0.88-1.00 accuracy).

claims.claim: Style bias is strongest precisely on technical content (math, factual QA, coding) and weakest on creative writing, and the paper recommends normalizing formatting before judging technical-heavy evaluation sets — directly applicable to a code-review judge, which evaluates exclusively technical output.
claims.quote: First, style bias is consistently strongest for technical content (math, factual QA, coding) and weakest for creative writing. [...] The per-topic decomposition reinforces the recommendation in Section 5 to normalize formatting before judging if your evaluation set is technical-heavy.

claims.claim: Aider runs a linter on each source file after every LLM edit and offers an automatic fix loop, implementing a deterministic post-edit gate as a shipped feature (not a proposal).
claims.quote: Aider now lints your code after every LLM edit, and offers to automatically fix any linting errors.

claims.claim: LLMs handle source-code line numbers poorly, frequently making off-by-one and similar errors even when given fully numbered code listings, so raw linter output keyed to line numbers (e.g. flake8's 'app.py:23:36: F821') is a bad feedback format for LLMs.
claims.quote: LLMs are quite bad at working with source code line numbers, often making off-by-one errors and other mistakes even when provided with a fully numbered code listing.

claims.claim: Reformatting lint errors by using tree-sitter to obtain the AST and displaying each error line highlighted inside its containing function/method/class makes LLMs more effective at fixing the error — a claim asserted by the author without benchmark data in this post.
claims.quote: Aider augments the raw linter by displaying and highlighting the lines that have errors within their containing functions, methods, classes. To do this, aider uses tree-sitter to obtain the code’s AST and analyzes it in light of the linting errors. LLMs are more effective at editing code that’s provided with context like this.

claims.claim: A language-agnostic baseline linter can be built purely from tree-sitter parsing: aider detects syntax and other fatal errors across most popular programming languages by locating the ERROR nodes tree-sitter inserts into the AST, requiring no per-language linter installation.
claims.quote: When tree-sitter encounters a syntax error or other fatal issue parsing a source file, it inserts an AST node with type `ERROR`. Aider simply uses these `ERROR` nodes to identify all the lines with syntax or other types of fatal error, and displays them in the LLM friendly format described above.

claims.claim: Aider's lint-fix feedback loop is iterative: it sends the LLM a report of lint errors, requests changes, and repeats the cycle multiple times until issues are resolved — an early instance of the multi-round verify-and-repair loop pattern.
claims.quote: If so, aider will send the LLM a report of the lint errors and request changes to fix them. This process may iterate a few times as the LLM works to fully resolve all the issues.

claims.claim: Un pipeline simple y determinista de tres fases (localización, reparación, validación de parche) —sin dejar que el LLM decida acciones futuras ni opere herramientas complejas— superó en SWE-bench Lite a todos los agentes de software open source existentes en el momento de la publicación, logrando 32.00% (96 fixes correctos) con un coste medio de $0.70 por issue.
claims.quote: Our results on the popular SWE-bench Lite benchmark show that surprisingly the simplistic Agentless is able to achieve both the highest performance (32.00%, 96 correct fixes) and low cost ($0.70) compared with all existing open-source software agents!

claims.claim: La arquitectura de Agentless elimina deliberadamente la autonomía agéntica: el flujo se estructura en fases fijas de localización, reparación y validación de parche, en lugar de un loop abierto donde el LLM planifica sus propias acciones — evidencia de que estructurar fases con un gate de validación puede rendir más que la orquestación agéntica compleja.
claims.quote: Agentless employs a simplistic three-phase process of localization, repair, and patch validation, without letting the LLM decide future actions or operate with complex tools.

claims.claim: SWE-bench Lite contiene problemas defectuosos como benchmark: issues cuya descripción incluye el parche ground-truth exacto o descripciones insuficientes/engañosas; los autores construyeron SWE-bench Lite-S excluyéndolos para una evaluación más rigurosa — advertencia empírica al citar cifras de SWE-bench Lite sin filtrar.
claims.quote: we manually classified the problems in SWE-bench Lite and found problems with exact ground truth patch or insufficient/misleading issue descriptions. As such, we construct SWE-bench Lite-S by excluding such problematic issues to perform more rigorous evaluation and comparison.

claims.claim: Los autores sostienen que la complejidad de los enfoques basados en agentes, combinada con las limitaciones de los LLMs de la época (mediados de 2024), pone en duda que los agentes autónomos complejos sean necesarios, y proponen que técnicas simples e interpretables sirvan como baseline para el desarrollo autónomo de software.
claims.quote: the complexity of these agent-based approaches, together with the limited abilities of current LLMs, raises the following question: Do we really have to employ complex autonomous software agents? [...] Our work highlights the current overlooked potential of a simple, interpretable technique in autonomous software development.

claims.claim: El agente no tiene ninguna herramienta aparte de bash y ni siquiera usa la interfaz de tool-calling de los LMs; en lugar de implementar herramientas ad hoc, se confía en que el modelo explote el shell — un dato clave contra la hipótesis de que añadir muchas herramientas especializadas (LSP, AST, etc.) es imprescindible para el rendimiento en benchmarks.
claims.quote: Does not have any tools other than bash — it doesn't even need to use the tool-calling interface of the LMs. This means that you can run it with literally any model.

claims.claim: El agente usa un historial completamente lineal sin compaction ni procesadores de historia: cada paso solo añade mensajes, de modo que la trayectoria y el contexto pasado al LM son idénticos — relevante para la palanca de context engineering: la compaction/aislamiento de contexto no fue necesaria para lograr >74% en SWE-bench Verified.

claims.claim: Cada acción se ejecuta con subprocess.run de forma independiente (sin sesión de shell con estado), lo que según los autores hace trivial el sandboxing (basta cambiar subprocess.run por docker exec) y mejora la estabilidad del agente — patrón de diseño relevante para ejecución aislada y verificación reproducible en galaxy-brain.

claims.claim: Anthropic's SWE-bench Verified state-of-the-art result (49% with upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet, vs. 45% prior SOTA) was achieved with a deliberately minimal scaffold: just a prompt, a Bash tool, and a file Edit tool, sampling until the model decides it is done or hits the 200k context limit — no hardcoded workflow or discrete phase transitions.
claims.quote: Our design philosophy when creating the agent scaffold optimized for updated Claude 3.5 Sonnet was to give as much control as possible to the language model itself, and keep the scaffolding minimal. The agent has a prompt, a Bash Tool for executing bash commands, and an Edit Tool, for viewing and editing files and directories. We continue to sample until the model decides that it is finished, or exceeds its 200k context length. This scaffold allows the model to use its own judgment of how to pursue the problem, rather than be hardcoded into a particular pattern or workflow.

claims.claim: Agent scaffolding is a first-order performance lever independent of the model: SWE-bench measures the model-plus-scaffold system, and performance varies significantly with scaffold design even when the underlying model is held constant.
claims.quote: SWE-bench doesn't just evaluate the AI model in isolation, but rather an entire "agent" system... The performance of an agent on SWE-bench can vary significantly based on this scaffolding, even when using the same underlying AI model.

claims.claim: Holding the scaffold fixed, model capability dominated the score differences: with the exact same agent scaffold, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) scored 49%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (old) 33%, and Claude 3 Opus 22% on SWE-bench Verified — a checkable table published in the post.
